query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating tungsten powders with a controlled, thin few‐layer graphene film prior to copper chemical plating and sintering produces a graphene-enhanced tungsten–copper interface that reduces thermal boundary resistance. This intervention increases the overall thermal conductivity of W–Cu composites while retaining their mechanical durability and irradiation resistance under fusion-reactor joint conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Chemically plated W–Cu composite powders prepared by current methods (e.g., as in PMC12028711) where tungsten particles are uniformly coated with copper to form a three‐dimensional Cu network after sintering.
generation.intervention: Introduce a single processing step: deposit a uniform, few-layer graphene coating on tungsten powders before the copper plating process. This can be achieved through a scalable method (e.g., chemical vapor deposition or solution-phase exfoliation with subsequent deposition) that forms a nanoscale graphene interlayer.
generation.conditions: Sintering to be performed at optimized temperatures (around 1350 °C) and times in an inert atmosphere so that the graphene layer is preserved (i.e., not oxidized or excessively degraded), while the copper network forms uniformly. The composite would then be evaluated under high-heat flux and fusion reactor simulated irradiation conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous graphene interlayer at the tungsten–copper interfaces that bridges the phases, ensuring improved interfacial contact and electron/phonon coupling.
generation.mechanism: Graphene has an exceptionally high in-plane thermal conductivity (often exceeding 2000 W/mK). By inserting a thin, well-bonded graphene layer between tungsten and copper, the thermal boundary resistance is reduced. This promotes more efficient electron and phonon transport across the interface. Moreover, due to its inherent strength and chemical stability, the graphene interlayer should not compromise mechanical durability or irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The graphene-modified W–Cu composite is expected to show an increase in overall thermal conductivity (on the order of roughly 10–15% improvement, though with some uncertainty) compared to a conventional W–Cu composite. Mechanical strength and irradiation resistance will remain comparable to (or possibly be slightly enhanced relative to) the baseline composite.
generation.baseline: A conventional chemically plated and sintered W–Cu composite (as prepared following current powder-based methods without graphene pre-coating) wherein the connectivity of the copper network is established solely by sintering-induced copper slip and densification.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect depends sensitively on the graphene layer’s thickness and quality. If the layer is too thick, it could act as an thermal insulator; if it is discontinuous or degrades during sintering, the interface improvement may be lost. Process parameters must be carefully optimized to avoid detrimental effects such as altered pore formation or compromised interfacial bonding.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends findings from two separate domains: the established role of sintering temperature in promoting a uniform copper network in W–Cu composites (PMC12028711::web::014) and molecular simulation and experimental studies showing enhanced thermal conductance at Cu/graphene interfaces (PMC9654340::web::014). The uncertainty lies in whether the integration of a graphene interlayer can be achieved without interfering with the copper network formation and whether the known advantages of graphene in Cu composites will directly translate in the W–Cu system.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using identical chemical plating and sintering conditions: one set using standard tungsten powders and one set where tungsten powders are pre-coated with a few-layer graphene film. After sintering, subject both sets to identical mechanical (e.g., hardness, compressive strength) and thermal tests (e.g., laser flash analysis for thermal conductivity) as well as simulated fusion reactor irradiation testing (using ion irradiation to specified fluences). Analyze the microstructure and interfacial bonding using electron microscopy.
measurements: Overall thermal conductivity (via laser flash or comparable method)
Vickers/ nanoindentation hardness and compressive strength
Damage assessment under irradiation (defect density, irradiation-induced changes)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the graphene-enhanced samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., greater than ~10% increase) in thermal conductivity over the baseline samples, or if they exhibit any reduction in mechanical durability or irradiation resistance (as evidenced by diminished strength or increased defect formation), then the hypothesis is considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, the metallized diamond/Cu composite coating was fabricated by supersonic laser deposition. The microstructure and interface at different laser powers were studied. The effect of laser on the thermal conductivity of the coating was explained. The laser irradiation elevated the diamond content in the coating and improved the bonding interface. The laser intensifies the degree of the plastic deformation of the Cu, resulting in the formation of a coating with higher density, reducing the defects at the micro-interface and helping to improve the thermal conductivity. The crystallinity is slightly increased under the action of the laser, which can also contribute to the improvement of the thermal conductivity. The metallized micro-interface improved the non-wettability of diamond and copper under the action of laser, elevated the heat transfer efficiency at the interface, and reduced the degree of work hardening. The coating prepared at a laser power of 1000 W has the highest thermal diffusion coefficient of 89.3 mm2/s and thermal conductivity of 313.72 W/(m·K), which is 8.92% higher compared to the coating prepared without laser. In summary, the interfacial thermal conductivity of the copper–graphene interface was systematically studied by means of MD simulations. The key findings are concluded as follows. First, the thermal conductivity of the interface decreases with the increase in the number of graphene layers. Compared with single-layer graphene, the thermal conductivity of n-layer (n > 5) graphene decreases by about 78%. The underlying mechanism is that the increase in graphene layers enhances phonon scattering, which weakens the phonon coupling between copper and graphene in the low-frequency region. Second, Cu(011)/Gr possesses the highest TBC (673.61 MW/m2K), which has an increment of 4.2% and 5.2%, compared with the values of the Cu(001)/Gr (640.19 MW/m2K) and Cu(111)/Gr (644.41 MW/m2K) models, respectively. The effect of atomic structures can be clarified through the potential energy distribution, which indicates that a higher energy barrier within the interface means stronger interfacial bonding and is good for phonon transmission.
